body:
From invention to practical use

A new invention may originate in a university, government laboratory, company or individual workshop. However, creating an invention and making it widely available are different activities. A laboratory may develop a useful water-purification method but lack the facilities, finance or distribution network needed to manufacture equipment for thousands of households. Another organisation may have those facilities but not possess the necessary technology.

Technology transfer is the process through which technical knowledge, skills, processes or inventions are made available to another person or organisation for further development or practical application. It can involve written instructions, practical training, technical assistance, confidential know-how and intellectual property rights. Technology transfer is therefore broader than the sale of a patent.

Commercialisation means converting an invention, research result or other intellectual property into a product, service or commercially useful process. Commercialisation may involve licensing, manufacturing partnerships, investment, further development or the formation of a new enterprise.

Why intellectual property matters

Intellectual property (IP) consists of legally protected creations of the mind. Different forms of IP protect different subject matter. A patent protects a qualifying invention; copyright protects original expression; trademarks distinguish goods or services; and confidential know-how may be protected through secrecy and contractual obligations.

In India, Section 48 of the Patents Act, 1970 gives a patent owner specified exclusive rights. For a patented product, these include the right to prevent unauthorised making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing of that product in India. For a patented process, protection covers unauthorised use of the process and, for the product directly obtained through it, unauthorised use, offering for sale, sale or importation for those purposes in India.

These are principally rights to exclude others. A patent does not itself guarantee permission to market a medicine, operate a factory or use inventions covered by somebody else's patents. Other patents, safety rules and regulatory approvals may still apply. Patent protection is also territorial: an Indian patent does not automatically confer enforceable patent rights in every other country.

Assignment and licensing are different legal transactions

FeatureAssignmentLicensing
Basic meaningTransfer of ownership of specified IP rightsPermission to use specified IP rights
Ownership after transactionPasses to the assignee to the extent assignedNormally remains with the licensor
Person receiving rightsAssigneeLicensee
Typical considerationAgreed sale price or other considerationRoyalty, fee, other benefit or agreed royalty-free use

Suppose a research institution owns a patent for a water-purification device. If it assigns the entire patent to a manufacturer, the manufacturer becomes its owner. If it licenses the patent, the manufacturer receives permission to undertake activities specified in the licence while the institution normally retains ownership.

Both arrangements can help research reach users. Assignment may suit a complete transfer of a business or technology portfolio. Licensing is particularly useful when the original owner wishes to retain rights while allowing another organisation to develop, manufacture or distribute the invention.

Protection and access must work together

IP protection can encourage investment by allowing innovators to obtain returns from successful research. At the same time, overly restrictive licensing or poor availability can prevent useful knowledge from reaching society. Technology-transfer policy therefore concerns both incentives to innovate and access to the resulting technology.

Prelims focus

  • Technology transfer may include knowledge, training, know-how and legal rights.
  • An assignment transfers ownership; a licence grants permission within an agreed scope.
  • Section 48 of the Patents Act, 1970 specifies the exclusive rights of a patentee.
  • Patent rights are territorial and do not replace other regulatory approvals.
  • Trap: Commercialisation does not necessarily require selling ownership of the patent.

[Sources: WIPO, IP Assignment and Licensing, sections on assignment and licensing, consulted 14 November 2026; Patents Act, 1970, Section 48; NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, Chapter 4, Globalisation and the Indian Economy, printed pages 56–58.]

title: Intellectual Property Rights and the Meaning of Technology Transfer

body:
What a licence permits

A licence is permission granted by an intellectual property right holder to another party to undertake activities that would otherwise require the holder's consent. The right holder is the licensor; the person or organisation receiving permission is the licensee.

A patent licence might permit a company to manufacture and sell a patented device. A different licence might permit only research use, production of components or sale within a particular geographical market. The precise rights depend on the agreement.

Exclusive, sole and non-exclusive licences

The most important distinction concerns whether the same rights may be exercised by other persons.

TypePosition of the licenseePosition of the licensor
ExclusiveReceives the specified rights to the exclusion of others within the licensed scopeIs excluded from exercising those specified rights within that scope
SoleIs the only outside licensee for the specified scopeMay continue using the IP but cannot appoint additional licensees for that scope
Non-exclusiveMay use the IP alongside other authorised usersMay continue using the IP and license it to others

Indian patent law expressly defines an exclusive licence in Section 2(1)(f) of the Patents Act, 1970 as one that grants specified rights to the exclusion of all other persons, including the patentee. Exclusivity can be limited to a field of use, territory or defined rights; it need not cover every possible use of the invention.

For example, a university might give one firm an exclusive licence to use an invention in agricultural equipment while permitting other firms to use it in household products. The field of use must be clearly identified to determine what each firm may do.

Important terms in a licensing agreement

A well-defined agreement normally addresses the following matters:

  • Subject matter: Which patent, technology, documentation or know-how is covered?
  • Permitted acts: May the licensee manufacture, use, sell, distribute or conduct research?
  • Territory: In which countries or markets does the permission apply?
  • Duration: How long does the permission continue, and when may it end?
  • Exclusivity: May the licensor use the technology or license other parties?
  • Payment: Is there an initial fee, recurring royalty, milestone payment or other agreed consideration?
  • Sub-licensing: May the licensee authorise another person to use the technology?
  • Responsibilities: Who must provide technical assistance, maintain confidentiality, report sales or meet agreed performance requirements?

A cross-licence is an arrangement in which 2 parties permit one another to use specified IP rights. This can be useful when each party needs access to inventions controlled by the other. It is distinct from a simple one-way licence.

Royalties and other payments

A royalty is compensation for permitted use of intellectual property. It may be calculated as an agreed amount per unit produced or sold, a percentage of specified sales, or another agreed measure. Payments may also include an upfront lump sum or an amount due when development or commercial milestones are reached.

Illustrative royalty calculation

If a licence requires a royalty of Rs 20 for each licensed device sold and the licensee sells 100 devices, the royalty is Rs 2,000. This is a contractual example, not a statutory royalty rate.

Some licences are royalty-free. Others combine an initial payment with later royalties. The existence of a licence does not imply that a particular royalty formula or payment rate is compulsory.

Requirements under Indian patent law

Under Section 68 of the Patents Act, 1970, an assignment, licence or other specified interest in a patent must be recorded in a written, duly executed agreement embodying the terms and conditions governing the parties' rights and obligations. Section 69 provides for registration of title or notice of an interest in the patent register. Contractual permission and the recording of legal interests should therefore not be confused.

Prelims focus

  • The licensor grants permission; the licensee receives it.
  • An exclusive patent licence excludes others, including the patentee, from the specified licensed rights.
  • A sole licence permits continued use by the licensor but prevents additional outside licensees for the same scope.
  • A non-exclusive licence allows multiple licensees.
  • Section 68 requires a written and duly executed patent assignment or licence agreement.
  • Trap: An exclusive licence is not the same as an assignment of ownership.

[Sources: WIPO, IP Licensing Strategies for Ventures, sections on exclusive, sole and non-exclusive licences and drafting terms, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, IP Assignment and Licensing, consulted 14 November 2026; Patents Act, 1970, Sections 2(1)(f), 68 and 69.]

title: Licensing Agreements, Royalties and the Scope of Technology Use

body:
Why universities transfer technology

Universities and public research laboratories produce knowledge through scientific investigation. Some results contribute mainly to education or further research. Others can be developed into useful products, processes or services. Commercialisation helps connect these results with organisations capable of manufacturing, investment, testing and distribution.

A public laboratory may develop a method of reducing water contamination. A private manufacturer may possess production facilities and a distribution network. A properly structured licence can allow the manufacturer to develop and supply products while the research institution retains the agreed intellectual property rights.

This relationship can benefit both sides. Industry obtains access to research-based technology, while the institution may receive royalties, sponsored research opportunities or evidence that its work is reaching users. Society may gain access to an improved product or service.

Who owns inventions made in a university?

Ownership must be established from the applicable law, employment terms, institutional policy, research contract and funding conditions. It is incorrect to assume that every discovery belongs automatically to the researcher who performed the experiment or that every publicly funded invention must be available without conditions.

Different arrangements are possible. A university may own a patent and license it to an industrial partner. A research contract may allocate ownership between collaborating parties. Some results may be released openly, whereas others may require protection or confidentiality before disclosure.

From research result to industrial adoption

Where patent protection is appropriate, a research institution may follow this general sequence:

  1. Identify and disclose the invention: Researchers explain the result, possible applications and contributors to the institution's responsible office.
  2. Assess protection and ownership: The institution examines patentability, existing rights, contractual obligations and whether public disclosure could affect protection.
  3. Evaluate practical usefulness: Technical feasibility, expected users, costs and possible commercial partners are considered.
  4. Select a transfer arrangement: An institution may license technology, enter a research collaboration, assign rights where appropriate or support a new enterprise.
  5. Develop and deploy: The receiving organisation undertakes further development, necessary approvals, production and distribution.

Publicly describing an invention before obtaining appropriate protection can damage the novelty required for a patent in many circumstances. However, patenting is not obligatory for every research result. Publication, open dissemination and non-exclusive licensing may be more suitable where broad access is the main objective.

National Research Development Corporation

The National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) was established by the Government of India in 1953. It functions under the administrative control of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR), Ministry of Science and Technology. Its principal objective is to promote, develop and commercialise technologies, know-how, inventions, patents and processes arising from national research institutions and universities.

NRDC provides an example of a public institution connecting research organisations with potential industrial users. It is a technology-development and commercialisation organisation, not the authority that grants patents.

Gujarat connection: GUJCOST and IP facilitation

The Gujarat Council on Science and Technology (GUJCOST), under the Government of Gujarat's Department of Science and Technology, operates an Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre (IPFC) at Gandhinagar. The centre was established in collaboration with the Government of India's Department of Science and Technology.

IPFC provides guidance and facilitation relating to patents and other IP, including awareness, patent searches, filing support and commercialisation. GUJCOST also supports institutional IP Cells, which can help collect invention disclosures and provide first-level guidance to students and faculty. These bodies facilitate protection and transfer; they do not replace the statutory patent examination and grant process.

GUJCOST's IP commercialisation support seeks to connect promising innovations with assessment, potential partners and pathways towards licensing or market adoption. Such support is particularly relevant to students, researchers, startups and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in Gujarat.

Balancing research income and public benefit

Public institutions may seek financial returns from licensing, but income is not their only objective. They may also consider affordability, access to publicly useful technologies, research freedom and the ability of licensees to develop an invention successfully. For some technologies, licensing several manufacturers may spread benefits more widely than giving one firm exclusive access. For others, limited exclusivity may help attract the investment needed for development.

Prelims focus

  • NRDC was established in 1953 and operates under DSIR.
  • NRDC promotes commercialisation of technologies from research institutions and universities.
  • GUJCOST's Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre is located at Gandhinagar.
  • University IP ownership depends on the applicable legal and contractual arrangements.
  • IP facilitation and patent granting are different functions.
  • Trap: Public funding does not by itself establish that every invention is automatically free for unrestricted commercial use.

[Sources: NRDC, About NRDC, institutional history and objectives, consulted 14 November 2026; GUJCOST, Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre, IP Cell and IP Commercialisation pages, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, technology-transfer and licensing guidance, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, Chapter 4, printed pages 56–58.]
